claims.claim: Gregory visited her about nine months after Basil's death, after the council of Antioch, and found her dying on a sack on a board
claims.witness: Gregory of Nyssa, Life (clarke1916 l.184-192); Clarke's dates, 379 (l.52)

claims.claim: Eldest child; named for her grandmother, who confessed Christ in the persecutions
Her father chose a husband for her about her twelfth year; he died and she refused other suitors
She drew Basil from the pride of oratory to the ascetic life
claims.witness: Gregory of Nyssa, Life (l.136), one witness with an interest. Gregory of Nazianzus (Or. xliii, through Blomfield Jackson, npnf208 l.1252-1264) says Basil had already resolved on it; Jackson gives both

claims.claim: She persuaded her mother to live as an equal with her maids
The household was a double monastery, women under Macrina and men under her brother Peter of Sebaste
claims.witness: W. K. Lowther Clarke, introduction (l.78-80)

claims.claim: She took in children exposed by the roadside in famine
claims.witness: Life (l.264)

claims.claim: On the Soul and the Resurrection gives her teaching in dialogue form
claims.witness: Gregory of Nyssa (npnf205 l.38086-38200); Moore and Wilson, preface (l.247-250) and note 1747 (l.40780-40782, probably composed 380)

claims.claim: Her dying prayer

contested_claims.claim: Whether Macrina turned Basil to the ascetic life
contested_claims.sides: Gregory of Nyssa, Life (l.136): Basil came home proud of his oratory and Macrina drew him to philosophy and the life of toil. Gregory of Nazianzus, Or. xliii, as Blomfield Jackson reports him (npnf208 l.1252-1256): Basil had already determined to renounce the world. Jackson (l.1256-1264) gives both and reads Macrina as giving Basil the resolution to carry out his determination.

contested_claims.claim: The size of the family
contested_claims.sides: Life (l.132, 212): four sons and five daughters, the estate divided in nine parts. Clarke, introduction (l.44): ten children, of whom four sons and five daughters survived infancy. Moore and Wilson, npnf205 (l.490-492): the father left ten children, five sons and five daughters.

absent_details.detail: Year of birth
absent_details.note: Not given in any held source; the scan's c.327 is not used.

absent_details.detail: Writings of her own
absent_details.note: None held; her words come only as Gregory records them in the Life and the dialogue.

absent_details.detail: How much of the dialogue's argument is hers
absent_details.note: Neither Gregory nor Moore and Wilson say; told as Gregory's written form.

claims.claim: Ulfila took him as a pupil from his earliest years, from his parents, taught him Scripture and raised him like a son
claims.witness: Auxentius 55 (Kauffmann l.15234-15238)

claims.claim: Bishop of Durostorum (Silistria) in Lower Moesia
claims.witness: Kauffmann l.3397; title of the letter; Maximinus 140 ('Dorostorensi', l.16231)

claims.claim: Ulfila held the see of Durostorum before him
claims.witness: Kauffmann's view (l.3434-3435, 3479)

claims.claim: Distinct from Auxentius of Milan; alive when Maximinus wrote
claims.witness: Maximinus, Dissertatio 140 (Kauffmann l.16230-16231)

claims.claim: His letter survives inside Maximinus's defence of Palladius and Secundianus against Ambrose, written in the margins of Ambrose's On the Faith in Paris cod. lat. 8907, a fifth-century manuscript that also holds Hilary of Poitiers
claims.witness: Kauffmann l.485-512 (margins of the first book of Ambrose's De fide, l.509-512), 683-692 (margin text begins after Hilary ends at fol. 297'), 686-715; Streitberg l.613-634

claims.claim: The margin hand dates probably to the sixth century
claims.witness: Kauffmann following Traube and Hauler (l.741-753)

claims.claim: Sent from Constantinople soon after Ulfila's death; its readers the Arians of Moesia
claims.witness: Kauffmann n. 3 (l.3474-3479): with Bessell on the place and time of sending; the Moesian readers are Kauffmann's own view. Bessell and Jülicher: written for Theodosius

claims.claim: Ready to join Palladius of Ratiaria in public debate
claims.witness: Maximinus 140 (Kauffmann l.16233-16236)

contested_claims.claim: How much of the fragment is Auxentius's own wording
contested_claims.sides: W. Luft: only to 'in fide educauit' (P 306'), the rest Maximinus's excerpt from another work. Kauffmann: one uniform biblical style throughout, unlike Maximinus (l.3480-3494).

contested_claims.claim: Who the letter was written for
contested_claims.sides: Bessell and A. Jülicher: for Theodosius. Waitz and Kauffmann: not; Kauffmann (with Bessell on the place and time) looks to the Arians of Moesia (l.3474-3479).

contested_claims.claim: When the margin text was written
contested_claims.sides: Waitz and Pertz: 381-384. Bessell: after 438. Delisle: second half of the fifth century. Traube, Hauler, Kauffmann: probably the sixth (l.741-753).

absent_details.detail: His birth, death and years as bishop
absent_details.note: No vendored source gives them.

absent_details.detail: The letter's address, opening and close
absent_details.note: Lost (Kauffmann l.3455-3456; Streitberg l.632). The title is Kauffmann's.

claims.claim: Bishop among the Goths for seven years, then driven out by persecution under a Gothic judge with a great crowd of confessors, crossed the Danube and was received with honour by Constantius
claims.witness: Auxentius of Durostorum, Letter 58-59 (Kauffmann l.15271-15286); a pupil writing in praise

claims.claim: His forebears were Cappadocian captives taken by Gothic raiders under Valerian and Gallienus, from Sadagolthina near Parnassus
claims.witness: Philostorgius II.5 in Photius's epitome (Walford l.120); one partisan witness through a hostile epitomator

claims.claim: The emperor called him the Moses of his day
claims.witness: Philostorgius II.5 (Walford l.120)

claims.claim: Made bishop at thirty from the rank of reader
claims.witness: Auxentius 56 (Kauffmann l.15240-15241); Kauffmann l.3766-3768 also reads Philostorgius this way

claims.claim: Born 311, consecrated 341, crossed 348-349, died June 383 aged 72
claims.witness: Friedrich Kauffmann's reconstruction from Auxentius's numbers (Kauffmann l.3740-3765, 3702-3725)

claims.claim: Made letters for the Goths and translated the Scriptures except the Books of Kings
claims.witness: Philostorgius II.5 (Walford l.120); Socrates IV.33 on the letters (npnf202 l.14448-14451)

claims.claim: The surviving Gothic Bible fragments are the remains of Ulfila's translation
claims.witness: Wilhelm Streitberg 1908, introduction (Streitberg l.603-607): fragments carry no translator's name but there can be no doubt

claims.claim: Taught that the Father alone is unbegotten and true God, the Son God and creator of all yet subordinate, rejected homoousios and homoiousios
claims.witness: Auxentius 42-51 (Kauffmann l.15111-15180); the deathbed creed 63 (l.15302-15318, 'Ego Ulfila episkopus et confessor')

claims.claim: Preached forty years in Greek, Latin and Gothic and left treatises in all three
claims.witness: Auxentius 53-54 (Kauffmann l.15211-15226)

claims.claim: Held the Nicene faith until he signed the creed of Constantinople in 360
claims.witness: Socrates II.41 (npnf202 l.9608-9612)

claims.claim: Joined the Arians later, under Valens, pressed by the needs of an embassy or, possibly, thinking their view better
claims.witness: Sozomen VI.37 (npnf202 l.40158-40171)

claims.claim: Went to Constantinople when the emperor summoned the bishops, expecting a council and meaning first to debate the Pneumatomachi; fell ill and died there, leaving a written creed
claims.witness: Auxentius 61-63 (Kauffmann l.15283-15304), read with Kauffmann (l.3702-3706), who follows Sievers against Bessell's reading that he went at the emperor's command for the debate (n. 2, l.3718-3719); Kauffmann dates it June 383

contested_claims.claim: When and how Ulfila came to the Homoian faith
contested_claims.sides: Auxentius (pupil, partisan): he always believed so, in his deathbed creed. Socrates II.41: Nicene as Theophilus's disciple until he signed at Constantinople in 360. Sozomen VI.37: took part in 360 without leaving Nicaea, joined the Arians later under Valens, compelled by the embassy or thinking it better.

contested_claims.claim: Whether Ulfila was the Goths' first bishop
contested_claims.sides: Philostorgius II.5 (via Photius) calls him their first bishop. Socrates II.41 names Theophilus, bishop of the Goths, who signed at Nicaea, and makes Ulfila his disciple.

contested_claims.claim: When the Goths of Ulfila crossed into the empire
contested_claims.sides: Auxentius 59: after seven years as bishop, under Constantius (Kauffmann: 348-349). Sozomen VI.37: Ulfila led the embassy when the Goths crossed fleeing the Huns, under Valens.

contested_claims.claim: Who consecrated him and when
contested_claims.sides: Philostorgius II.5: Eusebius and the bishops with him, under Constantine. Kauffmann emends to Constantius and the synod of Antioch 341, and thinks he was first a chorbishop.

absent_details.detail: Ulfila's own treatises and interpretations in Greek, Latin and Gothic
absent_details.note: Auxentius says he left many; none is identified in the Library.

absent_details.detail: Whether the deathbed creed was left in Latin as it survives
absent_details.note: Kauffmann reports Waitz's doubt (l.3736-3738); no witness settles it.

absent_details.detail: The see of the Eusebius who consecrated Ulfila
absent_details.note: Philostorgius II.5 says only 'Eusebius and the other prelates' (Walford l.120); Kauffmann speaks of 'Eusebius und die Eusebianer' and the Eusebian synod of Antioch 341 (l.3767-3769, 3809-3811) without naming the consecrator's see. Left as the bare name on the card.

claims.claim: Succeeded Liberius as bishop of Rome after a disputed election with Ursinus
claims.witness: Socrates IV.29; Sozomen VI.23; Gesta inter Liberium et Felicem (Avellana 1); Ammianus XXVII.3.12-13. The year (366 or 367) is in the contested record

claims.claim: On one day 137 dead bodies were found in the Basilica of Sicininus, and Damasus won through the efforts of his partisans
claims.witness: Ammianus Marcellinus XXVII.3.13 (outside witness, most likely a pagan per Yonge's preface l.750-752; one source for the figure)

claims.claim: Ursinus, a deacon, could not bear his defeat and had bishops of little note ordain him in secret
claims.witness: Socrates IV.29 (following Rufinus, per Zenos's note); Sozomen VI.23 (after Socrates and Rufinus, per Hartranft's note)

claims.claim: Damasus paid charioteers, arena men and gravediggers and besieged a basilica, killing 160 of the people with none dead on his side
claims.witness: Gesta inter Liberium et Felicem (Avellana 1), anonymous, from Ursinus's party; one partisan witness

claims.claim: His Roman councils condemned Auxentius of Milan and held to the creed of Nicaea; he condemned Timothy, follower of Apollinarius, by the judgment of the apostolic see
claims.witness: Damasus, synodal letters in Theodoret II.17, V.10, V.11

claims.claim: Jerome helped him with his letters and answers to councils of East and West
claims.witness: Jerome, Letter 123.10 (npnf206)

claims.claim: Damasus asked Jerome to revise the Old Latin Gospels against the Greek
claims.witness: Jerome, Preface to the Four Gospels (npnf206)

claims.claim: Priscillian, Instantius and Salvianus came to Rome to clear themselves and were not admitted to his presence
claims.witness: Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.48 (one witness)

claims.claim: Wrote verse in heroic metre; died under Theodosius at almost eighty
claims.witness: Jerome, Lives 103

contested_claims.claim: Who was to blame for the violence of the 366 election
contested_claims.sides: Ammianus Marcellinus, an outside witness and most likely a pagan, blames both rivals, says Damasus won by his partisans' efforts and counts 137 dead in one day. Socrates of Constantinople blames Ursinus for a secret ordination and schism, and Sozomen tells it the same way after him. The anonymous Gesta, from Ursinus's party, blames Damasus for hired violence and counts 160 dead in a besieged basilica, none on his side.

contested_claims.claim: The year of his accession and of his death
contested_claims.sides: Accession 366 (Gesta's consuls; Hartranft's note on Sozomen) against 367 (Jerome's Chronicle, per Zenos's note on Socrates). Death December 384 (chronological tables in Fremantle's Jerome) against 380 (Richardson's note to Lives 103).

absent_details.detail: Birthplace and family
absent_details.note: Zenos's note on Socrates IV.29 calls him 'a Spaniard by race, native of Mantua'; no early witness used here gives his birthplace or family. Left out of the brief.

absent_details.detail: The martyr shrines and epigrams in the catacombs
absent_details.note: Census names his epigram on Sixtus II (Ferrua edition, not vendored). The Library carries only Jerome's line on his verse and Jackson's note quoting Northcote and Brownlow; kept to the card.

claims.claim: A Spanish layman of noble birth and great wealth, ascetic in habit, who drew many followers
claims.witness: Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.46 (hostile to him and to his accusers)

claims.claim: Condemned in his absence by a council at Saragossa
claims.witness: Sulpicius II.47; denied by Priscillian, Liber ad Damasum (Tractate II)

claims.claim: Made bishop of Abila by Instantius and Salvianus
claims.witness: Sulpicius II.47 (Halm's Latin 'in Abilensi oppido'); Jerome, Lives 121 ('bishop of Abila')

claims.claim: Went to Rome to clear himself before Damasus and was not admitted; Ambrose also opposed him
claims.witness: Sulpicius II.48; Priscillian's own appeal to Damasus (Tractate II)

claims.claim: Tried twice by the prefect Evodius, found guilty and put to death at Treves by order of Maximus, about 385
claims.witness: Sulpicius II.50-51; Jerome, Lives 121; year from Richardson's note

claims.claim: Did not deny that he had given himself up to lewd doctrines, held night meetings with women and prayed naked
claims.witness: Sulpicius II.50 only; hostile; reports the court of Evodius

claims.claim: Taught that souls came down from God through circles of evil powers into bodies, and joined the patriarchs' names to parts of the body
claims.witness: Orosius, Commonitorium 2 (hostile); like teachings cursed in his name by Braga I, canons 6, 9, 10 (hostile, later)

claims.claim: Cursed anyone who did not condemn Mani and the Manichaeans, and the Patripassians
claims.witness: Priscillian, Liber apologeticus (Tractate I)

claims.claim: Martin of Tours begged Maximus not to shed blood and objected to a secular judge in a church case
claims.witness: Sulpicius II.50

claims.claim: After his death his followers honoured him as a martyr, buried the dead in Spain with great pomp and swore by his name
claims.witness: Sulpicius II.51 (one witness)

claims.claim: The eleven Wurzburg treatises are his
claims.witness: Georg Schepss 1889, from the names in Tractates I and II; the manuscript carries no author's name

contested_claims.claim: Whether the council at Saragossa condemned Priscillian
contested_claims.sides: Sulpicius Severus: sentence was passed against Instantius, Salvianus, Helpidius and Priscillian in their absence. Priscillian, Liber ad Damasum: none of his group was accused, convicted or condemned there, and Damasus's own letter had forbidden judging the absent and unheard.

contested_claims.claim: Whether he was a Gnostic or Manichaean heretic
contested_claims.sides: Sulpicius Severus calls his teaching the heresy of the Gnostics; Orosius calls him worse than the Manichaeans; Braga I (561) curses teachings 'as Manichaeus and Priscillian said'. Jerome of Strido reports both the accusation and his defenders' denial. Priscillian's own Liber apologeticus curses the Manichaeans and other heresies.

absent_details.detail: Year of birth, parents and schooling
absent_details.note: No source used here gives them; the scan's 'c.340' has no held witness and is not used.

absent_details.detail: Magic practised from boyhood
absent_details.note: Sulpicius reports it only as something 'believed'; kept to the card as his report.

claims.claim: A cross of light appeared over Jerusalem, from Calvary to the Mount of Olives, when Cyril had followed Maximus as bishop; people ran to the church; Cyril wrote to the emperor
claims.witness: Sozomen IV.5 (npnf202 l.32769-32800); Gifford, introduction ch. I, from Cyril's letter (npnf207 l.764-767, 826-835)

claims.claim: The letter to Constantius is dated 7 May 351
claims.witness: Gifford (npnf207 l.764-767), from the letter, which is not held

claims.claim: As a priest he gave the Catechetical Lectures to candidates for baptism in Lent of 348
claims.witness: Gifford, introduction ch. IX, following Touttée (npnf207 l.4125-4379); Jerome, Lives 112 (lectures composed while a young man)

claims.claim: He gave the creed to be learned by heart, since not all could read the Scriptures
claims.witness: Cyril, Catechetical Lecture V.12 (npnf207 l.8808-8862)

claims.claim: The party of Acacius of Caesarea ejected Maximus and put Cyril in his place
claims.witness: Socrates II.38 (npnf202 l.8968-8975); Sozomen IV.20 (l.34143)

claims.claim: Cyril renounced his priestly orders from Maximus to be made bishop by the Arians, and later degraded Heraclius
claims.witness: Jerome, Chronicle, as quoted by Gifford (npnf207 l.640-660); hostile witness, one source

claims.claim: The synod at Constantinople in 382 declared Cyril canonically ordained by the bishops of the province
claims.witness: Synodical letter in Theodoret V.9 (npnf203 l.16041-16044)

claims.claim: In a famine Cyril sold the church's veil and ornaments to feed the poor; Acacius used this as a pretext to depose him
claims.witness: Sozomen IV.25 (npnf202 l.34700-34730), who says he inquired and found these the facts

claims.claim: Cyril refused for two years to answer Acacius's summons, and appealed to the emperor after his deposition
claims.witness: Socrates II.40 (npnf202 l.9430-9445)

claims.claim: Driven from his see three times, about 357, in 360 and about 367
claims.witness: Gifford, introduction ch. I (npnf207); Socrates II.42, II.45; Sozomen IV.25; Jerome, Lives 112 (often expelled)

claims.claim: In 381 Cyril accepted the homoousion, having retracted his former opinion
claims.witness: Socrates V.8 (npnf202 l.15085-15092); Sozomen VII.7 (l.40793-40795, renounced the Macedonian tenets); rejected by Gifford and Touttée (npnf207 l.1326-1336)

claims.claim: He held his see eight years under Theodosius and died in 386
claims.witness: Jerome, Lives 112 (npnf203 l.41500-41505); Gifford's reckoning with the Roman Martyrology (npnf207 l.1360-1370)

claims.claim: The Mystagogic Lectures are Cyril's
claims.witness: Gifford, introduction ch. XI, following Touttée and Milles; some manuscripts name John of Jerusalem (npnf207 l.5167-5300)

contested_claims.claim: How Cyril became bishop
contested_claims.sides: Socrates II.38 and Sozomen IV.20: the party of Acacius ejected Maximus and installed Cyril. Jerome's Chronicle (hostile; as Gifford quotes it): Cyril renounced his ordination by Maximus to be made bishop by the Arians, and degraded Heraclius, whom Maximus had installed. The synod of 382 (Theodoret V.9): canonically ordained by the bishops of the province. Gifford (who defends Cyril) calls Socrates's and Jerome's accounts irreconcilable and both improbable, and follows Reischl: designated in Maximus's lifetime, then canonically consecrated.

contested_claims.claim: Why Acacius deposed Cyril
contested_claims.sides: Sozomen IV.25: the famine sale of the church's veil and ornaments, used as a pretext. Socrates II.40: he does not know the charges; Cyril stayed away two years from fear. Theodoret II.22: Acacius seized some small occasion; II.23 gives Acacius's charge of a robe sold to a stage dancer.

contested_claims.claim: Whether Cyril changed his doctrine before 381
contested_claims.sides: Socrates V.8 (retracted his former opinion and accepted homoousion); Sozomen VII.7 (renounced Macedonian tenets). Against: Touttée and Gifford, from the lectures, which teach the Son's unity of essence with the Father without the word.

contested_claims.claim: Authorship of the Mystagogic Lectures
contested_claims.sides: Some manuscripts (Augsburg/Munich, as Gifford reports) name John, bishop of Jerusalem; Rivet and Aubertin in the seventeenth century attacked them. Gifford, following Touttée and Milles, holds Cyril wrote all the lectures, since Cat. XVIII.33 promises them.

contested_claims.claim: Cyril's prophecy on the rebuilding of the Temple under Julian
contested_claims.sides: Socrates III.20: he foretold it, and an earthquake followed. Gifford: no satisfactory evidence he foretold a miracle, though he may well have expected failure; Rufinus's account seems a conjecture from Cat. XV.15.

absent_details.detail: Birth, parents and schooling
absent_details.note: No source used here gives them. Gifford reckons a birth about 315 or a little before from what Cyril seems to have seen of the holy places. One relative is named: Gifford names his sister's son Gelasius, whom Cyril made bishop of Caesarea (npnf207 l.586-588); Theodoret names Gelasius of Caesarea too (npnf203 l.15861). Given on the card, not in the brief.

absent_details.detail: The text of the Letter to Constantius
absent_details.note: Not held in the Library in any vendored file found; known here through Gifford's account and Sozomen IV.5.

absent_details.detail: Jerome's Chronicle
absent_details.note: The Latin continuation is not held (the Fotheringham Chronicle file carries the Eusebian canons); the passage is used as Gifford quotes it.

claims.claim: Father and son Apollinaris, priest and reader, stayed at Epiphanius the sophist's recitation of a hymn to Dionysus; Theodotus expelled them and restored them after penance
claims.witness: Sozomen VI.25 (npnf202 l.38992-39095); Lietzmann, part I (l.722-760)

claims.claim: The younger Apollinaris was born at Laodicea to a father from Alexandria who had taught at Berytus
claims.witness: Socrates II.46 (npnf202 l.9921-9935); Lietzmann (l.722-730)

claims.claim: George of Laodicea excommunicated him, in 346 by Lietzmann's date
claims.witness: Sozomen VI.25 (for receiving Athanasius); Socrates II.46 (for the friendship with Epiphanius, or George's wavering creed); Lietzmann l.800-812 and chronology l.~495

claims.claim: Under Julian's ban, Scripture was rewritten in Greek literary forms
claims.witness: Socrates III.16 (father and son; npnf202 l.11222ff); Sozomen V.18 (the son alone; l.36656ff); Lietzmann judges Sozomen more credible (l.2564-2576)

claims.claim: He taught that the divine Word took the place of the human mind in Christ
claims.witness: Socrates II.46 (l.9955-9961); Gregory of Nazianzus, Ep. 202 (npnf207 l.44530-44540); Theodoret V.3 (npnf203 l.15446-15460); his own fragment 81, from the Apodeixis, kept by Gregory of Nyssa and Justinian (Lietzmann l.11480-11492)

claims.claim: His followers kept the Nicene teaching on the Trinity
claims.witness: Socrates II.46 (l.9961-9965); Schaff's note in npnf214 (l.14084ff)

claims.claim: His followers formed their own churches and sang his songs at work and at the loom
Condemned at Rome under Damasus, in the presence of Peter of Alexandria, in 377 by Lietzmann's date
claims.witness: Sozomen VI.25; Damasus's letter in Theodoret V.10 (npnf203 l.16066-16120); Lietzmann chronology (l.~566); Hartranft's note at Sozomen VI.25 (npnf202 l.39034) gives 377 after Rade and 374 after Hefele

claims.claim: The Apollinarians were anathematized in canon 1 of Constantinople 381
Jerome heard him lecture at Antioch
claims.witness: Jerome, Ep. 84.3 (npnf206 l.18997-19000); Lietzmann dates it 374

claims.claim: His dogmatic works were destroyed; some survived under the names of Athanasius, Julius and Felix of Rome and Gregory Thaumaturgus
claims.witness: Lietzmann, part III (l.4080-4160)

claims.claim: He was bishop of Laodicea
claims.witness: Jerome, Lives 104 (npnf203 l.41390-41396); Lietzmann (l.818-825; perhaps a rival bishop from 360)

claims.claim: He died in the reign of Theodosius
claims.witness: Jerome, Lives 104; Lietzmann says the year is not known (l.3484-3490)

contested_claims.claim: Who wrote the Scripture paraphrases under Julian
contested_claims.sides: Socrates III.16: the father (Moses in heroic verse, the historical books) and the son (the Gospels as Platonic dialogues). Sozomen V.18: one Apolinarius only, whom Lietzmann takes for the son (an epic of Hebrew antiquities in twenty-four parts, comedies, tragedies, odes); Sozomen does not mention the Moses verse or the Gospel dialogues. Lietzmann finds Sozomen's account the more credible and allows the grammar to the father.

contested_claims.claim: Why George of Laodicea excommunicated him
contested_claims.sides: Sozomen VI.25: for receiving Athanasius into communion. Socrates II.46: for continuing the friendship with Epiphanius, or, as some affirm, because the Apollinarii separated over George's wavering creed. Lietzmann: October 346, at Athanasius's passage, and the earlier expulsion under Theodotus aimed at their pro-Nicene stance.

contested_claims.claim: What Apollinaris taught about Christ's flesh and soul
contested_claims.sides: Socrates II.46: first a body without soul, then a soul without reason. Gregory of Nazianzus, Ep. 202: flesh eternal, Godhead passible. Theodoret V.3: he varied. Ullman (cited by Browne and Swallow, npnf207 l.44400-44420): Gregory may have exaggerated the pamphlet.

absent_details.detail: Year of birth
absent_details.note: No held source gives it. The scan's c.310 is not used.

absent_details.detail: Year of death
absent_details.note: Lietzmann: unknown; Jerome says under Theodosius; Gregory of Nyssa's Antirrheticus (after 385) presumes him living. Richardson's note to Lives 104 gives about 390 (npnf203 l.41393).

absent_details.detail: An English text of his own words
absent_details.note: None held; fragments are Greek with Lietzmann's German, so the brief tells fragment 81 in modern words and does not quote it.

claims.claim: An African Donatist writer of the latter half of the fourth century
claims.witness: Gennadius, Lives 18; Augustine, On Christian Doctrine III.30 and Letter 93.43; Burkitt 1894

claims.claim: Wrote the Book of Rules, seven rules for reading Scripture, whose preface promises keys and windows into the secret places of the law
claims.witness: Tyconius, Liber Regularum (Burkitt's Latin); preface quoted in Augustine, On Christian Doctrine III.30

claims.claim: Wrote in defence of the Church against his own party, reported a Donatist council that received traditors without rebaptism, and was answered and warned by Parmenian, yet stayed with the Donatists
claims.witness: Augustine, Letter 93.43-44 (a Catholic bishop who wrote against the Donatists, an opponent of his party; one witness for the council report)

claims.claim: Augustine judged his staying with the Donatists, while arguing for a church spread through the world, 'a most inconsistent disposition', and says Parmenian checked him only on that ground
claims.witness: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine III.30; Letter 93.44 (an opponent of his party)

claims.claim: Augustine judged the third rule faulty for holding faith to be our own, and warned the book must be read with caution as a Donatist's, while commending it
claims.witness: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine III.30, III.33

claims.claim: Explained the whole Apocalypse in a spiritual sense
claims.witness: Gennadius, Lives 18

claims.claim: The Apocalypse commentary is lost but much of it survives in Primasius, Bede and Beatus
claims.witness: F. C. Burkitt 1894, after Haussleiter 1886

claims.claim: Wrote before 383
claims.witness: F. C. Burkitt 1894, from the 350-year reckoning in Rule 5 ('it would seem')

absent_details.detail: Birth, death, home town, and whether he was ordained
absent_details.note: Not given in the sources used here. The scan's 'lay writer' rests on no held line naming him a layman; the card role is 'Donatist writer' (flagged to coordinator).

absent_details.detail: Condemnation by a Donatist council around 380
absent_details.note: Named in the census and the Burkitt file's vendoring header, not in any held source text; Augustine reports only Parmenian's reply and warning.

absent_details.detail: Tyconius's own case for staying a Donatist
absent_details.note: No writing of his on that choice survives in the sources used here; his Bellum Intestinum has perished (Burkitt). Augustine's verdict is recorded as Augustine's in the claims.

claims.claim: Presented the Eunomian creed to Theodosius at the 383 gathering; Theodosius kept only the homoousian creed
Came from Cappadocia and studied with Aetius at Alexandria
claims.witness: Philostorgius III.20 (Walford l.188); Socrates IV.7 says he was Aetius's secretary (npnf202 l.12461)

claims.claim: His father was a poor farmer who carved alphabet letters; he learned shorthand
claims.witness: Gregory of Nyssa, Against Eunomius I (npnf205 l.3365-3376); one hostile witness

claims.claim: Made bishop of Cyzicus
claims.witness: Philostorgius V.3 (under Constantius); Socrates IV.7, Sozomen VI.26 (under Valens)

claims.claim: Left Cyzicus after his clergy accused him
claims.witness: Philostorgius VI.1-3 (l.246-250); Socrates IV.7 (l.12492-12496); Sozomen VI.26 (l.39133-39146)

claims.claim: Taught that God is the Unbegotten Substance, the Son begotten by the Father's will when he was not, unlike in substance; rejected homoousios as division
claims.witness: Eunomius, Apology VII, XV, XI, XXIV, XXVI (Whiston l.38, 58, 48, 94, 98)

claims.claim: Basil wrote against the Apology; Gregory against the Apology for the Apology
claims.witness: Philostorgius VIII.12 (l.316); Gregory of Nyssa, Against Eunomius I (npnf205 l.3495-3505)

claims.claim: Banished by Theodosius; died soon after and was buried at Dacora, his birthplace
claims.witness: Sozomen VII.17 (npnf202 l.41523-41533); Philostorgius X.6 (Walford l.382) has him living at his country place, the Dacoroenian fields, after his banishments

claims.claim: The prefect Eutropius later had him moved from the Dacoroenian territory to Tyana, to be kept by monks, and would not let his body lie in his master's tomb
claims.witness: Philostorgius XI.5 (Walford l.410); one partisan witness through a hostile epitomator

claims.claim: Taught that God knows no more of his own substance than we do
claims.witness: Socrates IV.7 (npnf202 l.12515-12519); one hostile witness. The words are not found in the held Apology (Whiston), which does not speak to the point either way

contested_claims.claim: When he became bishop of Cyzicus
contested_claims.sides: Philostorgius V.3 and Theodoret (per A. C. Zenos's note, npnf202 l.12486-12490): under Constantius. Socrates IV.7 and Sozomen VI.8: under Valens.

contested_claims.claim: Why he left Cyzicus
contested_claims.sides: Philostorgius: won over Constantinople's clergy, then refused Eudoxius's demands and went home. Socrates: driven out by the people. Sozomen: Eudoxius found no fault; Eunomius refused to return to people who suspected him.

contested_claims.claim: Whether he first taught baptism by single immersion
contested_claims.sides: Some in Sozomen VI.26 say so; Sozomen thinks Theophronius and Eutychius began it.

contested_claims.claim: How Basil died
contested_claims.sides: Philostorgius VIII.12: of remorse after reading Eunomius's first book against him. Photius: a falsehood.
